propositions.text: On October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended off Vancouver Island with 76 Tamil passengers from Sri Lanka seeking refugee status without legal documentation.
propositions.quote: On October 17, 2009, a vessel called the Ocean Lady was apprehended off the west coast of Vancouver Island, in British Columbia. Seventy-six people, among them the appellants, were aboard. All were Tamils from Sri Lanka. They claimed to have fled Sri Lanka because their lives were endangered in the aftermath of the civil war in that country. They asked for refugee status in Canada. None had the required legal documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that on October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers without legal documentation.

propositions.text: The Crown claims the four appellants were organizers of the voyage and that passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 each.
propositions.quote: The Crown claims that the four appellants — the captain and chief crew of the vessel — were the organizers of the venture. The Crown alleges that the majority of passengers each paid, or promised to pay, $30,000 to $40,000 for the voyage.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown alleges the four appellants organized the voyage and passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 each.

propositions.text: The appellants were charged under s. 117 of IRPA for organizing or aiding illegal entry into Canada, with possible imprisonment and refugee disqualification.
propositions.quote: The appellants were charged under s. 117 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (“IRPA ”), which makes it an offence to “organize, induce, aid or abet” the coming into Canada of people in contravention of the IRPA . Consequences of conviction could include lengthy imprisonment and disqualification from consideration as a refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants were charged under s. 117 IRPA for organizing illegal entry, risking imprisonment and refugee disqualification.

propositions.text: The appellants challenged s. 117's constitutionality for infringing s. 7 Charter rights, arguing it criminalizes humanitarian aid and family assistance.
propositions.quote: Before their trial, the appellants challenged the constitutionality of s. 117 of the IRPA , on the ground that it infringes the right to life, liberty and security of the person enshrined in s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms . The trial judge ruled that the provision was unconstitutional because it criminalized not only organized people smuggling, but helping close family members to come to Canada and humanitarian assistance to refugees.

propositions.text: The trial judge found s. 117 unconstitutional for criminalizing humanitarian aid and family assistance.
propositions.quote: The trial judge ruled that the provision was unconstitutional because it criminalized not only organized people smuggling, but helping close family members to come to Canada and humanitarian assistance to refugees.

propositions.text: The British Columbia Court of Appeal reversed the trial judge and found s. 117 constitutional.
propositions.quote: The British Columbia Court of Appeal reversed that decision, and found the provision to be constitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argued s. 117 infringed s.7 Charter rights; the trial judge agreed but the Court of Appeal reversed, upholding constitutionality.

propositions.text: Section 117 is unconstitutional insofar as it permits prosecution for humanitarian aid, mutual asylum-seeker assistance, or family assistance.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I conclude that, insofar as s. 117 permits prosecution for humanitarian aid to undocumented entrants, mutual assistance amongst asylum-seekers or assistance to family members, it is unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is unconstitutional when it permits prosecution for humanitarian aid, mutual asylum-seeker assistance, or family assistance.

propositions.text: Canadian authorities intercepted the Ocean Lady with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers from Sri Lanka, boarded in Indonesia and Thailand, none with proper documentation.
propositions.quote: Canadian authorities intercepted the freighter ship Ocean Lady offshore of Vancouver Island. They found 76 passengers aboard; all were Tamil asylum-seekers from Sri Lanka who had boarded the ship in Southeast Asia: 24 boarded the ship in Indonesia between June and August 2009, and 52 in Thailand in September 2009. None of the 76 migrants had the proper documentation to enter Canada.

propositions.text: Most migrants agreed to pay $30,000 to $40,000, with $5,000 down payment before boarding and the rest after arrival.
propositions.quote: Most had agreed to pay a sum of between $30,000 and $40,000 to come to Canada. Typically, down payments of $5,000 were exacted prior to boarding, together with undertaking a debt of another $25,000 to $35,000 to be paid subsequent to arrival in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states authorities intercepted 76 Tamil asylum-seekers without documents; most agreed to pay $30,000-$40,000 with down payments.

propositions.text: The Crown alleges the four appellants were key organizers and chief crew of a for-profit smuggling operation from Southeast Asia to Canada.
propositions.quote: The four appellants, Francis Anthonimuthu Appulonappa, Hamalraj Handasamy, Jeyachandran Kanagarajah and Vignarajah Thevarajah, are alleged to have been the point persons for a transnational for-profit operation to smuggle undocumented migrants from Southeast Asia to Canada. They are said to have been responsible for organizing the asylum-seekers in Indonesia and Thailand prior to boarding the freighter, and serving as the chief crew of the ship on the voyage to Canada — Mr. Handasamy as captain, Mr. Thevarajah as chief engineer, and Mr. Kanagarajah and Mr. Appulonappa as key crew members.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown alleges the four appellants organized and crewed a for-profit smuggling operation from Southeast Asia to Canada.

propositions.text: The appellants were charged under s. 117(1) IRPA, prohibiting knowingly organizing or aiding entry of persons without required documents.
propositions.quote: The appellants were charged with the offence of “Organizing entry into Canada” found in s. 117 of the IRPA , which, at the relevant time, provided: 117. (1) No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants were charged under s. 117(1) IRPA for knowingly organizing or aiding entry without required documents.

propositions.text: IRPA was amended in 2012, replacing s. 117(1) and adding subsections; the current s. 117 is not before the court.
propositions.quote: The IRPA was amended by the Protecting Canada’s Immigration System Act, S.C. 2012, c. 17, ss. 41(1) and 41(4) , whereby s. 117(1) was replaced by a new subsection and two subsections were added, which came into force on December 15, 2012. Section 117 as it was at the time of the alleged offences of the appellants is therefore no longer in force. The constitutionality of the current s. 117 is not before us.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA was amended in 2012; the current s. 117 is not at issue here.

propositions.text: The appellants applied for a declaration that s. 117 is unconstitutionally overbroad, not contesting its application to their case.
propositions.quote: The appellants brought an application before Silverman J. on a voir dire for a declaration that s. 117 of the IRPA is unconstitutionally overbroad. They did not contend that s. 117 is unconstitutional as it applies to the allegations against them, which are that they were part of a for-profit smuggling operation.

propositions.text: They argued s. 117 is unconstitutional because it may convict humanitarian workers or family members assisting asylum-seekers, exceeding legislative intent and infringing s. 7 liberty.
propositions.quote: However, they argued that s. 117 is unconstitutional because it may lead to the conviction of humanitarian workers or family members assisting asylum-seekers for altruistic reasons. They argued that convicting people in these categories exceeds the legislative intent of s. 117 and infringes the guarantee of liberty contrary to the principle of fundamental justice against overbreadth. This violation of the liberty guarantee in s. 7 of the Charter was not justified under s. 1 of the Charter , they submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants sought a declaration that s. 117 is overbroad, arguing it may convict humanitarian or family helpers, violating s.7 Charter rights.

propositions.text: The Crown accepted s. 117's purpose excludes prosecuting family or humanitarian aid, but said s. 117(4) consent requirement prevents overbreadth.
propositions.quote: The Crown accepted that the purpose of s. 117 was not to convict persons helping close family members come to Canada or persons providing legitimate humanitarian aid to people coming to Canada. However, it argued that this did not render s. 117 overbroad because s. 117(4) of the IRPA required that the Attorney General of Canada authorize prosecution, which would allow him to screen out people in these categories.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown accepted s. 117 excludes family and humanitarian aid prosecutions, but said Attorney General consent prevents overbreadth.

propositions.text: Silverman J. found s. 117's purpose excludes prosecuting humanitarian or family aid, but s. 117 permits such prosecution, violating s.7 by overbreadth.
propositions.quote: Silverman J. concluded that, as the Crown contended, the purpose of s. 117 does not extend to prosecution of genuine humanitarian aid workers or family members. Because s. 117 permits the prosecution of such persons, it violates the s. 7 guarantee of liberty in a way that is overbroad, and hence not in accord with the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Silverman J. held s. 117 could not be read down to comply with the Charter and Attorney General consent does not save it from overbreadth.
propositions.quote: Silverman J. held that s. 117 could not be interpreted or “read down” to make it Charter compliant and that the prior consent to prosecution required by s. 117(4) does not save s. 117 from being unconstitutionally overbroad.

propositions.text: Silverman J. found the overbreadth was not justified under s. 1 and declared s. 117 inconsistent with s. 7 and of no force or effect, quashing indictments.
propositions.quote: Nor, in his view, was the overbreadth justified under s. 1 of the Charter . Silverman J. therefore declared s. 117 of the IRPA to be inconsistent with s. 7 of the Charter and hence of no force or effect under s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982 . He ordered that the indictments of the appellants be quashed: 2013 BCSC 198.

paragraphs.summary: Silverman J. found s. 117 overbroad and unconstitutional for prosecuting humanitarian or family aid, quashing indictments.

propositions.text: Before the Court of Appeal, the Crown changed position, arguing s. 117 aims to prevent all organizing or assisting unlawful entry, including family and humanitarian aid.
propositions.quote: Before the Court of Appeal, the Crown changed its submission on the purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA . It submitted that s. 117 was enacted to prevent all organizing or assisting of unlawful entry of others into Canada, including assistance to close family members and humanitarian assistance.

propositions.text: The Crown said this purpose furthers goals of controlling entry, protecting Canadians, preserving immigration integrity, and promoting international justice.
propositions.quote: This, the Crown said, was required to further Canada’s goals of (1) controlling who enters its territory; (2) protecting the health, safety, and security of Canadians; (3) preserving the integrity and efficacy of Canada’s lawful immigration and refugee claims regimes; and (4) promoting international justice and cooperation with other states on matters of security.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown changed its position, arguing s. 117 prevents all unlawful entry assistance, including family and humanitarian aid, to further Canada's goals.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal accepted the Crown's revised purpose and held s. 117 constitutional, noting Parliament rejected humanitarian exceptions due to definitional difficulties.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal accepted this revised submission as the purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA and on that basis held it to be constitutional. Neilson J.A. (Bennett and Hinkson JJ.A. concurring) concluded that Canadian laws criminalizing assistance to undocumented migrants have not historically allowed exceptions based on the offender’s motive or other characteristics. When the provision at issue was enacted in 1988, the question of whether humanitarian workers should be exempted received attention, but Parliament, concerned about “definitional difficulties” and “loopholes”, rejected creating an exception for these groups: para. 107. The purpose of s. 117 therefore aligned with its reach, and the provision was not overbroad.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal accepted the Crown's revised purpose and held s. 117 constitutional, rejecting humanitarian exceptions.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal held Attorney General consent under s. 117(4) guards against improper prosecutions on humanitarian or family grounds.
propositions.quote: The court added that the s. 117(4) requirement of the Attorney General’s consent to prosecute would guard against improper prosecutions on humanitarian grounds, family grounds or other grounds.

propositions.text: If Attorney General authorizes prosecution of humanitarian or family assistance, the issue is improper discretion, not overbreadth of s. 117(1).
propositions.quote: If the Attorney General were to authorize prosecution of people assisting close family members or providing humanitarian assistance, the vice would not be overbreadth of s. 117(1), but the improper exercise of ministerial discretion under s. 117(4) .

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found Attorney General consent guards against improper prosecutions; improper discretion, not overbreadth, would be the issue.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned invalidity declaration, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.
propositions.quote: In the result, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned the declaration of invalidity, set aside the acquittals and remitted the matter for trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned invalidity, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.

propositions.text: The IRPA governs immigration and refugee protection, aiming for fair procedures and upholding human rights, supported by international conventions.
propositions.quote: The IRPA (relevant provisions set out in Appendix A) is a complex statute dealing with the entry into Canada of foreign nationals through two processes — the immigration process and the refugee protection process. We are here concerned primarily with the refugee protection process. The IRPA aims to establish “fair and efficient [refugee] procedures that will maintain the integrity of the Canadian refugee protection system, while upholding Canada’s respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of all human beings”: s. 3(2)(e). Both goals are underpinned by Canada’s adhesion to international conventions and protocols, discussed more fully below.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains IRPA governs immigration and refugee protection, aiming for fair procedures and human rights, supported by international conventions.

propositions.text: A key concern is unauthorized entry threatening refugee system integrity; IRPA sanctions those helping unauthorized entry without documents.
propositions.quote: A significant concern for the integrity of Canada’s refugee protection system is the threat posed to it by the entry to Canada of unauthorized persons outside the lawful refugee regime. As part of combating this threat, the IRPA contains two provisions which sanction individuals for helping others to enter Canada without the documents required by border authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states unauthorized entry threatens refugee system integrity; IRPA sanctions those aiding entry without documents.

propositions.text: Section 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible those engaged in transnational people smuggling, preventing refugee claim determination.
propositions.quote: Section 37(1) (b) of the IRPA renders a person inadmissible to Canada where the person has “engag[ed], in the context of transnational crime”, in people smuggling, and, in effect, prevents that person’s refugee claim from being determined on its merits.

propositions.text: Section 117 creates an offence for knowingly organizing or aiding entry of persons without required documents.
propositions.quote: Section 117 , under the marginal note “Organizing entry into Canada”, creates an offence. At the relevant time, it read: 117. (1) No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act.[1]

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible people smugglers and s. 117 creates an offence for organizing entry without documents.

propositions.text: Sections 117(2) and (3) provide penalties; s. 121(1)(c) considers profit as an aggravating sentencing factor for s. 117 offences.
propositions.quote: Sections 117(2) and 117(3) provide penalties of imprisonment and fines. At the time of the charges at issue in this case, s. 121(1) (c) of the IRPA under the marginal note “Aggravating factors”, stipulated that committing the offence for profit was a fact to be considered in sentencing under s. 117 .[2]

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117(2) and (3) provide penalties and s. 121(1)(c) considers profit an aggravating factor in sentencing.

propositions.text: Subsection (4) requires Attorney General's consent to start prosecutions under s. 117.
propositions.quote: Subsection (4) provides a screening mechanism for instituting proceedings under s. 117 — prosecutions can proceed only with the consent of the Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that subsection (4) requires Attorney General's consent to start prosecutions under s. 117.

propositions.text: Unauthorized entry participation may lead to prosecution under s. 117 or inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b).
propositions.quote: participating in the unauthorized entry of other people into Canada may have two consequences under the IRPA . First, it may result in prosecution and imprisonment and/or substantial fines upon conviction under s. 117 . Second, it may render a person who engages in certain proscribed activities inadmissible to Canada under s. 37(1) (b).

propositions.text: This appeal concerns prosecution under s. 117; inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b) is addressed in companion appeals.
propositions.quote: The first consequence — prosecution under s. 117 — is the subject of this appeal. The second consequence — inadmissibility to Canada — is the subject of the companion appeals in B010 v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 58, [2015] 3 S.C.R. 704.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains unauthorized entry may lead to prosecution under s. 117 or inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b); this appeal concerns prosecution under s. 117.

propositions.text: Charter applies to foreign nationals entering Canada without required documents (Singh).
propositions.quote: The Charter applies to foreign nationals entering Canada without the required documentation: Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177.

propositions.text: Section 7 of the Charter protects life, liberty, and security of the person except in accordance with fundamental justice.
propositions.quote: Section 7 of the Charter provides: 7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Section 117 threatens liberty and engages s. 7 because it is a penal provision with potential life imprisonment (Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act).
propositions.quote: As a penal provision with potential sentences up to life imprisonment, it is clear that s. 117 of the IRPA threatens liberty and hence engages s. 7 of the Charter : Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 486, at p. 492.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that the Charter applies to undocumented foreign nationals and s. 117 threatens liberty engaging s. 7 of the Charter.

propositions.text: Does s. 117 of the IRPA infringe s. 7 liberty contrary to fundamental justice?
propositions.quote: The main issue before us is whether s. 117 of the IRPA threatens liberty, protected by s. 7 of the Charter , in a manner contrary to the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: If yes, is the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
propositions.quote: If the answer is yes, a second question arises: Is the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter ?

propositions.text: If not justified, what is the appropriate remedy for s. 117's constitutional infirmity?
propositions.quote: If the answer to this second question is no, a final question arises: What is the appropriate remedy for the constitutional infirmity in s. 117 ?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issues: whether s. 117 infringes s. 7 liberty, if justified under s. 1, and the remedy if not.

propositions.text: s. 117 violates s. 7 because it catches people assisting family or fleeing persecution outside its purpose, making it overbroad.
propositions.quote: The appellants contend that s. 117 violates s. 7 of the Charter because the provision catches two categories of people outside its purpose — people who assist close family members to come to Canada and humanitarians who assist those fleeing persecution to come to Canada, in each case without required documents.

propositions.text: s. 117 is overbroad, grossly disproportionate, unconstitutionally vague, and perpetuates inequality, offending fundamental justice.
propositions.quote: The appellants say that s. 117 is therefore overbroad, contrary to the principles of fundamental justice. They also argue that s. 117 offends the principles of fundamental justice because its impact on liberty is grossly disproportionate to the conduct it targets, because it is unconstitutionally vague, and because it perpetuates inequality.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 violates s. 7 by overbroadly catching family and humanitarian assistance and is disproportionate, vague, and perpetuates inequality.

propositions.text: Overbreadth occurs when law interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective (Bedford).
propositions.quote: A law is said to violate our basic values by being overbroad when “the law goes too far and interferes with some conduct that bears no connection to its objective”: Canada (Attorney General) v. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72, [2013] 3 S.C.R. 1101, at para. 101.

propositions.text: Overbreadth recognizes law may be rational in some cases but overreaches in others (Bedford, Carter).
propositions.quote: As stated in Bedford, “[o]verbreadth allows courts to recognize that the law is rational in some cases, but that it overreaches in its effect in others”: para. 113; see also Carter v. Canada (Attorney General), 2015 SCC 5, [2015] 1 S.C.R. 331, at para. 85.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains overbreadth as law interfering with unrelated conduct, recognizing rationality in some cases but overreach in others.

propositions.text: Overbreadth inquiry: determine law's object, then if it deprives s. 7 rights in cases not furthering that object.
propositions.quote: The first step in the overbreadth inquiry is to determine the object of the impugned law. The second step is to determine whether the law deprives individuals of life, liberty or security of the person in cases that do not further that object.

propositions.text: If law deprives s. 7 rights outside its object, it infringes fundamental justice.
propositions.quote: To the extent the law does this, it deprives people of s. 7 rights in a manner that infringes the principles of fundamental justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth analysis requires identifying the law's object and whether it deprives s. 7 rights outside that object, infringing fundamental justice.

propositions.text: s. 117 is overbroad as applied to other foreseeable situations, not just the appellants' conduct.
propositions.quote: The appellants argue that s. 117 is overbroad, not as it applies to the conduct alleged against them, but as it applies to other reasonably foreseeable situations.

propositions.text: Courts may consider reasonable hypotheticals to assess Charter consistency (Nur).
propositions.quote: It is indeed established that a court may consider “reasonable hypotheticals” to determine whether a law is consistent with the Charter : see R. v. Nur, 2015 SCC 15, [2015] 1 S.C.R. 773.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 is overbroad in foreseeable situations; courts may consider reasonable hypotheticals to assess Charter consistency.

propositions.text: First hypothetical: assisting close family members fleeing to Canada, e.g., parent with child or family on boat.
propositions.quote: The first scenario the appellants ask us to consider is the situation of a person assisting a close family member to flee to Canada. The appellants cite as examples a mother carrying her small child, or the father of a household taking his family dependants with him aboard a boat.

propositions.text: Mutual assistance among unrelated asylum-seekers is similar and reasonably foreseeable.
propositions.quote: This scenario could also encompass cases of mutual assistance among unrelated asylum-seekers. Indeed, refugees mutually assisting one another in their collective flight to safety is not meaningfully different from family members assisting one another and, as showed by the companion case B010, is a reasonably foreseeable situation.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants ask the court to consider assisting family or asylum-seekers fleeing to Canada as reasonably foreseeable scenarios caught by s. 117.

propositions.text: Second hypothetical: humanitarian aid to people fleeing persecution, by individuals or organizations, is a real and historical reality.
propositions.quote: The second scenario advanced by the appellants is the case of a person who, for humanitarian motives, helps people to flee from persecution. History is replete with examples of people who have aided others to flee persecution for humanitarian reasons. Sometimes the person is acting as an individual. Sometimes the person is a member of an organization devoted to helping people flee lands where they face threats and persecution. Church groups may help undocumented people find refugee protection in Canada: House of Commons Debates, vol. VII, 2nd Sess., 33rd Parl., August 12, 1987, at p. 8002 (Hon. Gerry Weiner, Minister of State (Immigration)). Humanitarian aid to fleeing people is not merely hypothetical; it is a past and current reality.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue humanitarian aid to persecuted people fleeing is a real, historical, and current reality caught by s. 117.

propositions.text: Overbreadth analysis depends on whether law's reach exceeds its object; first step is determining s. 117's object.
propositions.quote: As discussed, overbreadth analysis turns on whether the reach of the law exceeds its object. The first step is therefore to determine the object of s. 117 .

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth analysis requires determining s. 117's object as the first step.

propositions.text: Crown says s. 117's purpose is to catch all acts assisting undocumented migrants; thus not overbroad.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that the purpose of s. 117 is to catch all acts that in any way assist the entry of undocumented migrants. On this interpretation, s. 117 cannot be overbroad.

propositions.text: Appellants say 'human smuggling' has narrower purpose than Crown asserts, making s. 117 overbroad.
propositions.quote: The appellants, by contrast, submit that the offence of “human smuggling” has a narrower purpose than the Crown asserts, making it overbroad in catching all acts of assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s. 117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants; appellants say its purpose is narrower, making it overbroad.

propositions.text: Determining legislative purpose requires considering text, context, purpose statements, and international law.
propositions.quote: As with statutory interpretation, determining legislative purpose requires us to consider statements of legislative purpose together with the words of the provision, the legislative context, and other relevant factors: R. Sullivan, Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes (6th ed. 2014), at pp. 268-87; R. v. Chartrand, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 864, at pp. 879-82. Where legislation is enacted in the context of international commitments, international law may also be of assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains legislative purpose is determined by text, context, purpose statements, and international law.

propositions.text: Court agrees with appellants that s. 117's purpose is narrower than Crown asserts, aimed at combating people smuggling.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I agree with the appellants that the purpose of s. 117 is narrower than that asserted by the Crown.

propositions.text: Text is broad but purpose emerges from international instruments, statute context, legislative purpose, evolution, and debates.
propositions.quote: The text of s. 117 is admittedly broad. However, a narrow purpose emerges from (1) the international instruments to which Canada has subscribed; (2) the role of s. 117 in relation to the statute as a whole, in particular s. 37(1) ; (3) the IRPA ’s statements of legislative purpose; (4) the evolution of s. 117 ; and (5) the parliamentary debates.

propositions.text: True purpose of s. 117 is to combat people smuggling, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family assistance.
propositions.quote: Considering these indicia of purpose, it becomes evident that the true purpose of s. 117 is to combat people smuggling. The meaning of “people smuggling”, a term found in s. 37(1) (b) of the IRPA , is the subject of the companion case B010, and excludes mere humanitarian conduct, mutual assistance or aid to family members.

propositions.text: s. 117 violates the Charter by catching conduct outside its purpose, such as family or humanitarian assistance.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117 violates the Charter by catching these categories of conduct outside the provision’s purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117's purpose is narrower, aimed at people smuggling, excluding humanitarian or family aid, and s. 117 violates the Charter by catching such conduct.

propositions.text: Text of s. 117(1) prohibits knowingly organizing, inducing, aiding, or abetting entry of persons without required documents.
propositions.quote: At the relevant time, the text of s. 117 read as follows: 117. (1) [Organizing entry into Canada] No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act.

propositions.text: Penalties vary by number of persons involved, with fines and imprisonment up to life.
propositions.quote: (2) [Penalties — fewer than 10 persons] A person who contravenes subsection (1) with respect to fewer than 10 persons is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $500,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than 10 years, or to both, or (ii) for a subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than 14 years, or to both; and (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than two years, or to both.

propositions.text: For 10 or more persons, penalty is fine up to $1,000,000 or life imprisonment.
propositions.quote: (3) [Penalty — 10 persons or more] A person who contravenes subsection (1) with respect to a group of 10 persons or more is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction by way of indictment to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to life imprisonment, or to both.

propositions.text: No proceedings under s. 117 without Attorney General's consent (subsection 4).
propositions.quote: (4) [No proceedings without consent] No proceedings for an offence under this section may be instituted except by or with the consent of the Attorney General of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court recites s. 117's text, including prohibited conduct, penalties, and requirement of Attorney General's consent.

propositions.text: All agree s. 117(1) text is broad enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance.
propositions.quote: All agree that the text of s. 117(1) is broad enough to catch assistance to close family members and humanitarian assistance.

propositions.text: Doctrine of overbreadth recognizes state may use broader means than necessary to achieve legitimate objective (Heywood, Bedford, Carter).
propositions.quote: However, the doctrine of overbreadth recognizes that sometimes “the State, in pursuing a legitimate objective, uses means which are broader than is necessary to accomplish that objective”: R. v. Heywood, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 761, at p. 792; Bedford, at para. 101; Carter, at para. 85.

propositions.text: Failures of instrumental rationality require courts to look beyond text to determine if purpose is narrower (Bedford).
propositions.quote: The potential for “failures of instrumental rationality”, in which a given law is not a rational means to achieve a legislative objective, requires courts to go further than the text alone, and ask whether other considerations suggest Parliament’s purpose was narrower: Bedford, at para. 107.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) text is broad but overbreadth doctrine requires examining if purpose is narrower than text suggests.

propositions.text: Marginal note and subheading suggest s. 117 targets smuggling in organized crime, not humanitarian or family assistance.
propositions.quote: The marginal note of s. 117 , “Organizing entry into Canada”, read with the subheading “Human Smuggling and Trafficking”, while not to be accorded great weight (see Sullivan, at pp. 465-68), suggests that the provision is aimed at activity in connection with the smuggling of persons in the context of organized crime, as contrasted with providing humanitarian assistance or aiding close family members to enter a country without the required documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 117's marginal note and subheading suggest it targets organized crime smuggling, not humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Increased sanctions for groups of 10+ persons suggest focus on large-scale smuggling operations.
propositions.quote: Sections 117(2) and 117(3) also support the view that Parliament’s intent was to catch smuggling activity in the context of organized crime, rather than humanitarian, mutual or family assistance. These subsections provide for significantly increased sanctions based on the number of persons brought in.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds increased penalties for large groups support s. 117's focus on organized crime smuggling, not humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Requirement of Attorney General's consent suggests s. 117 not intended to convict everyone within broad ambit.
propositions.quote: Finally, the requirement in s. 117(4) that no prosecution occur without the Attorney General’s consent suggests that s. 117 was not intended to convict everyone who falls within s. 117(1)’s broad ambit, as discussed more fully below.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Attorney General's consent requirement suggests s. 117 not intended to convict all caught by broad text.

propositions.text: Legislation presumed to comply with Canada's international obligations; courts avoid interpretations violating them.
propositions.quote: As a matter of statutory interpretation, legislation is presumed to comply with Canada’s international obligations, and courts should avoid interpretations that would violate those obligations.

propositions.text: Courts interpret legislation reflecting values and principles of customary and conventional international law (Hape, Németh).
propositions.quote: Courts must also interpret legislation in a way that reflects the values and principles of customary and conventional international law: R. v. Hape, 2007 SCC 26, [2007] 2 S.C.R. 292, at para. 53; Németh v. Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 56, [2010] 3 S.C.R. 281, at para. 34.

propositions.text: IRPA s. 3 requires interpretation consistent with Canada's international obligations, including human rights instruments.
propositions.quote: Section 3 of the IRPA also requires that the IRPA be interpreted in a manner that complies with Canada’s international obligations, including “international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory”: s. 3(3) (f); see also s. 3(2) (b).

propositions.text: International instruments Canada has subscribed to shed light on s. 117's parliamentary purpose.
propositions.quote: The relevant international instruments to which Canada has subscribed should therefore shed light on the parliamentary purpose behind s. 117 of the IRPA .

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislation is presumed to comply with Canada's international obligations, which inform s. 117's purpose.

propositions.text: IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry assist align with Canada's international commitments in Refugee Convention, Organized Crime Convention, Smuggling Protocol, and Trafficking Protocol.
propositions.quote: The provisions of the IRPA relating to the fight against the assisting of unauthorized entry of persons to Canada respond to Canada’s international commitments related to these matters in the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, 189 U.N.T.S. 150 (“Refugee Convention”), the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2225 U.N.T.S. 209, the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2241 U.N.T.S. 480 (“Smuggling Protocol”), and the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2237 U.N.T.S. 319.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry assist align with Canada's international commitments in various UN conventions and protocols.

propositions.text: Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry by refugees who come directly from threatened territories and present themselves promptly with good cause.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Convention reflects humanitarian concerns. It provides that states must not impose penalties for illegal entry on refugees who come directly from territories in which their lives or freedom are threatened and who are present on the territory of the foreign state without authorization, “provided they present themselves without delay to the authorities and show good cause for their illegal entry or presence”: art. 31(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for refugees entering illegally if they promptly present themselves with good cause.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA exempts undocumented foreign nationals from illegal entry charges while refugee claims are pending.
propositions.quote: Consistent with this, s. 133 of the IRPA provides that foreign nationals who enter Canada without documents cannot be charged with illegal entry or presence while their refugee claims are pending.

propositions.text: Article 31(1) Refugee Convention grants immunity to genuine refugees entering illegally to seek refuge, including collective illegal entry aid.
propositions.quote: As I explain in B010, art. 31(1) of the Refugee Convention seeks to provide immunity for genuine refugees who enter illegally in order to seek refuge. For that protection to be effective, the law must recognize that persons often seek refuge in groups and work together to enter a country illegally. To comply with art. 31(1) , a state cannot impose a criminal sanction on refugees solely because they have aided others to enter illegally in their collective flight to safety.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.133 IRPA exempts undocumented refugees from charges while claims pending and article 31(1) protects collective illegal entry aid.

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol aims to combat migrant smuggling for financial/material benefit while protecting smuggled migrants' rights.
propositions.quote: The Smuggling Protocol is concerned with stopping the organized crime of people smuggling. It seeks to prevent and combat the smuggling of migrants and to promote cooperation among states to this end, while protecting the rights of smuggled migrants: art. 2.

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol requires criminalizing migrant smuggling for financial/material benefit as minimum offence definition.
propositions.quote: Article 6(1)(a) requires signatory states to adopt measures to establish migrant smuggling as a criminal offence. The Smuggling Protocol includes as a minimum definition for this offence, procuring illegal entry of a person into a state of which the person is not a national or a permanent resident, “in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit”: art. 3 (a).

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol not directed at family members or humanitarians; includes saving clause preserving other international law rights.
propositions.quote: As I explain in B010, the Smuggling Protocol was not directed at family members or humanitarians: paras. 60 and 68. Furthermore, while the Smuggling Protocol permits subscribing states to enact national laws criminalizing migration-related offences, it includes a “saving clause” that provides that nothing in the Smuggling Protocol “shall affect the other rights, obligations and responsibilities of States and individuals under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law”: art. 19(1).

propositions.text: Broad Crown interpretation of s.117 inconsistent with Smuggling Protocol's protection of smuggled migrants' rights.
propositions.quote: It would depart from the balance struck in the Smuggling Protocol to allow prosecution for mutual assistance among refugees, family support and reunification, and humanitarian aid. This suggests that the Crown’s broad interpretation of s. 117 ’s purpose is inconsistent with the Smuggling Protocol’s object of protecting the rights of smuggled migrants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Smuggling Protocol targets migrant smuggling for profit, excludes family/humanitarian aid, and Crown's broad s.117 view conflicts with it.

propositions.text: Statutory interpretation should harmonize international obligations to avoid conflict and respect all commitments.
propositions.quote: In dealing with conflicting statements of the legislative objects of a statute, the way forward lies in an interpretation which harmonizes obligations in the international instruments to which Canada is a party in a way that avoids conflict and gives expression to each of the various commitments.

propositions.text: Canada’s international commitments support s.117 targeting organized people smuggling, excluding humanitarian, mutual or family aid.
propositions.quote: I conclude that read together in this way, Canada’s international commitments support the view that the purpose of s. 117 is to permit the robust fight against people smuggling in the context of organized crime. This excludes criminalizing conduct that amounts solely to humanitarian, mutual or family aid.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes international commitments support s.117 targeting organized smuggling, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid.

propositions.text: Section 117 must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.
propositions.quote: Section 117 of the IRPA must also be read harmoniously with other provisions of the statute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.117 must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: Section 117 is under IRPA Part 3 'Enforcement', subheading 'Human Smuggling and Trafficking'; s.118 creates human trafficking offence.
propositions.quote: Section 117 of the IRPA falls under Part 3 of the IRPA , entitled “Enforcement”. Section 117 of the IRPA and the provisions that follow it fall under the subheading “Human Smuggling and Trafficking”. Section 118 creates the offence of human trafficking, leaving s. 117 , as noted, to constitute the offence of human smuggling.

propositions.text: Other IRPA references to smuggling/trafficking are in s.37(1)(b) rendering inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling or trafficking.
propositions.quote: The only other references in the IRPA to smuggling or trafficking are contained in s. 37(1) (b), which renders inadmissible to Canada a person who has engaged in smuggling or trafficking in persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.117 is under IRPA enforcement for human smuggling; s.118 covers trafficking; s.37(1)(b) bars inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling/trafficking.

propositions.text: Section 37(1)(b) targets conduct defined in Smuggling Protocol involving financial/material benefit and transnational crime context.
propositions.quote: As explained in B010, the conduct captured by s. 37(1) (b) is that which is set out in the Smuggling Protocol. In that context, people smuggling only occurs for “financial or other material benefit” and “in the context of transnational crime”.

propositions.text: Reading IRPA inadmissibility and enforcement provisions harmoniously shows s.117 targets organized smuggling for financial/material benefit, excluding humanitarian, mutual or family aid.
propositions.quote: Reading the inadmissibility and enforcement provisions of the IRPA harmoniously and as part of an integrated scheme therefore supports the view that the purpose of s. 117 is to penalize organizing or abetting illegal entry to Canada through acts knowingly connected to and furthering transnational organized crimes or criminal aims, to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit. This excludes humanitarian, mutual or family assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.37(1)(b) targets smuggling for profit in transnational crime; s.117 penalizes organized smuggling for benefit, excluding humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose within the legislation itself.
propositions.quote: The first, “most direct and authoritative evidence” of the legislative purpose of a provision is found in statements of purpose in the legislation itself — whether at the beginning of a statute, in the section in which a provision is found, or in sections providing interpretive guidelines: Sullivan, at pp. 274-76.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose within the legislation itself.

propositions.text: Refugee Convention aims to provide humanitarian refuge while protecting states' borders.
propositions.quote: In Febles v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 SCC 68, [2014] 3 S.C.R. 431, at paras. 29-30, this Court held that the Refugee Convention has the broad general aim of providing humanitarian refuge for those fleeing persecution while recognizing the need to protect states’ borders.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Febles confirming Refugee Convention balances humanitarian refuge and border protection.

propositions.text: IRPA's object provisions show both humanitarian refuge and border security goals are important.
propositions.quote: As discussed in B010, the object provisions of the IRPA establish that both of these broad goals are important to the IRPA as well.

propositions.text: Section 117 should be interpreted to balance security concerns and humanitarian aims of IRPA.
propositions.quote: It follows that s. 117 should be interpreted in a balanced way that respects both the security concerns as well as the humanitarian aims of the IRPA .

propositions.text: Interpreting s.117 to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants lets security concerns override humanitarian aims.
propositions.quote: An interpretation of s. 117 that catches all acts of assistance to undocumented migrants arguably allows security concerns to trump the humanitarian aims of the IRPA .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IRPA values both security and humanitarian aims; s.117 should balance these, not let security trump humanitarian goals.

propositions.text: Crown argues s.117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants to control borders for security, health, safety.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s view that the purpose of s. 117 is to catch all acts of assistance to undocumented migrants relies heavily on the fact that among the purposes of the IRPA is to control Canada’s borders to prevent migrants from entering the country illegally, for reasons of security, health and safety.

propositions.text: Controlling borders for security, health, safety is an important IRPA goal reflected in various objectives.
propositions.quote: To be sure, this is an important goal of the IRPA . It is reflected in the s. 3(2) (h) objective “to promote international justice and security by denying access to Canadian territory to persons, including refugee claimants, who are security risks or serious criminals”: see also s. 3(1) (i). It is likewise evinced by the aim “to protect the health and safety of Canadians and to maintain the security of Canadian society”: s. 3(2) (g); see also s. 3(1) (h).

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s.117 targets all assistance to undocumented migrants for border control; the court finds border security is an important IRPA goal.

propositions.text: 1988 amendments to Immigration Act added purposes including preserving access for genuine protection seekers, deterring illegal entry assistance, and responding to security concerns.
propositions.quote: A concern with security is also reflected in the specific legislative objects of An Act to amend the Immigration Act and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, R.S.C. 1985, c. 29 (4th Supp.), the statute which enacted what later became s. 117 of the IRPA (the “1988 amendments”): 1. The Immigration Act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 2 thereof, the following heading and section: Purposes of Amendments 2.1 . . . (a) to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims; (b) to control widespread abuse of the procedures for determining refugee claims, particularly in light of organized incidents involving large-scale introduction of persons into Canada to take advantage of those procedures; (c) to deter those who assist in the illegal entry of persons into Canada and thereby minimize the exploitation of and risks to persons seeking to come to Canada; and (d) to respond to security concerns, including the fulfilment of Canada’s obligations in respect of internationally protected persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes 1988 amendments aimed to preserve protection access, deter illegal entry assistance, and address security concerns.

propositions.text: The 1988 amendments also recognized humanitarian commitments to protect genuine protection seekers and concerns about exploitation and risks.
propositions.quote: The same statute, however, also recognized humanitarian commitments, including a stated objective “to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims” and concern for “exploitation” and risks to persons wishing to come to Canada: s. 1 , adding ss. 2.1(a) and 2.1(c).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the 1988 amendments also recognized humanitarian commitments and concerns about exploitation and risks.

propositions.text: IRPA's general objects include Canada's humanitarian ideals, saving lives, offering protection, and complying with international human rights instruments.
propositions.quote: The IRPA’s general objects further illustrate the importance of its broad humanitarian aims. Section 3(2)(c) speaks of “Canada’s humanitarian ideals”. The stated objects include “saving lives and offering protection to the displaced and persecuted” and “safe haven to persons with a well-founded fear of persecution”: ss. 3(2)(a) and 3(2)(d). Similarly, the objectives include striving to comply with “international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory”: s. 3(3)(f); see also s. 3(2)(b).

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA's objects include humanitarian ideals, saving lives, protection, and compliance with international human rights.

propositions.text: IRPA includes commitment to family reunification as a stated object.
propositions.quote: The IRPA also reveals a commitment to family, through stated objects of facilitating family reunification in Canada: s. 3(2)(f).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA's commitment to family reunification as a stated object.

propositions.text: Security goals do not supplant humanitarian aid and family unity; s.117 targets organized smuggling excluding humanitarian, mutual, family aid.
propositions.quote: In sum, while the security goals of the IRPA and the amendment that became s. 117 are important, they do not supplant Canada’s commitment to humanitarian aid and family unity. Both broad aims must be respected. This is accomplished by interpreting s. 117 as targeting organized smuggling operations having a criminal dimension, thereby excluding humanitarian, mutual and family aid.

propositions.text: Crown's broad s.117 interpretation would criminalize trivial humanitarian acts, incompatible with IRPA's refugee protection objects.
propositions.quote: Under the Crown’s interpretation of s. 117 , a father offering a blanket to a shivering child, or friends sharing food aboard a migrant vessel, could be subject to prosecution. This is incompatible with the refugee protection objects of the IRPA and the amendment that became s. 117 .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s.117 targets organized smuggling, excluding humanitarian aid; Crown's broad view criminalizes trivial aid, conflicting with IRPA's refugee protection.

propositions.text: Legislative history may assist in determining a provision's purpose.
propositions.quote: The legislative history of a provision may assist in determining its purpose: Sullivan, at pp. 286-87.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative history may help determine a provision's purpose.

propositions.text: Canada has criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, initially focusing on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship with little concern for migrants' plight.
propositions.quote: Canada has had laws criminalizing the assisting of undocumented migrants to enter the country since 1902. Early incarnations of the offence were focused on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship, with little concern for the plight of the migrants, who were typically expelled: An Act to amend the Immigration Act, S.C. 1902, c. 14, s. 2; Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1906, c. 93, ss. 65 and 66.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Canada criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, initially focusing on organizing illegal arrival with little concern for migrants.

propositions.text: 1919 amendment made it an offence to transport, harbour or conceal prohibited immigrants with summary conviction penalties; similar offences preserved in 1952 and 1976 Acts.
propositions.quote: In 1919, s. 12(4) of An Act to amend The Immigration Act, S.C. 1919, c. 25, made it an offence to transport into Canada, harbour or conceal the entry of prohibited immigrants. The provision was a summary conviction offence, with a maximum penalty of six months imprisonment and/or fines. Broadly similar offences were preserved in the 1952 and 1976 iterations of the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1919 amendment criminalized transporting or harboring prohibited immigrants with penalties; similar offences continued in later Acts.

propositions.text: In 1988, amendments introduced a new offence criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants with penalties based on scale.
propositions.quote: In 1988, “in light of organized incidents involving large-scale introduction of persons into Canada”, amendments introduced a new offence which, with minor changes, is the offence currently found in s. 117 of the IRPA

propositions.text: Greater culpability attached to large-scale breaches reflecting greater organizational activity.
propositions.quote: Thus, at the inception of what would become s. 117 , greater culpability already attached to large-scale breaches, reflecting greater organizational activity on the part of the accused or others with whom the accused acted in concert.

propositions.text: The offence included a screening mechanism requiring Attorney General's consent for proceedings under certain sections.
propositions.quote: The offence created in 1988 also included a new screening mechanism: no proceedings could be instituted under ss. 94.1 or 94.2 without the consent of the Attorney General

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the 1988 amendments criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants, with penalties scaled by number and requiring Attorney General consent.

propositions.text: The current s. 117 was part of the 2001 IRPA, preserving penalties and screening but increasing maximum penalties and adding sentencing guidance.
propositions.quote: The current s. 117 was part of a new comprehensive statute dealing with immigration and refugee protection, the IRPA , enacted in 2001. The offence remained substantially the same as previously, preserving the differing penalties based on scale, and the charge-screening mechanism. However, maximum penalties were significantly increased, while another provision was added to guide sentencing under the offence.

propositions.text: Section 121 guides sentencing considering bodily harm, criminal organization association, profit, and harm to migrants.
propositions.quote: Section 121 provided that in determining the penalty to be imposed under s. 117 , the court was to take into account (1) bodily harm or death to the migrant; (2) association with a criminal organization; (3) profit from the operation; and (4) harm to or degrading treatment of the migrants.

propositions.text: These changes followed the Smuggling Protocol requiring criminalization of smuggling for material benefit and aggravating circumstances.
propositions.quote: These changes came on the heels of the adoption of the Smuggling Protocol, which obliged state parties to criminalize the smuggling of migrants done for financial or other material benefit and to adopt legislative measures to establish aggravating circumstances such as harm to and degrading treatment of migrants

propositions.text: The second factor links smuggling to organized crime; first and fourth recognize more serious crime; third indicates profit or harm.
propositions.quote: The second factor in s. 121 reflected a more significant link between the offensive conduct and organized crime. The first and fourth factors recognized more serious crime. The third factor may be an indicator of either or both.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the 2001 IRPA's s. 117 and s. 121 provisions, increasing penalties and aligning with international smuggling protocols.

propositions.text: Prohibitions have focused on organized smuggling, increased penalties target organized crime, and s. 117 filters out innocent humanitarian or family aid.
propositions.quote: From this brief survey of the historical evolution of prohibitions on assisting the entry to Canada of undocumented people, I draw the following conclusions: (a) the prohibitions have, for over a century, focused on smuggling activity tied to organizing and furthering the illegal entry, not aid merely incidental to it; (b) successive revisions to the provision have coupled increased penalties with more precise targeting of organized crime-related smuggling activity, and the 2001 revision in particular followed in the footsteps of key developments in international law; and (c) s. 117 , from its inception in 1988 and as continued and revised by the IRPA in 2001, provided a filter to screen out assistance not associated with organized criminal smuggling, namely innocent humanitarian acts, mutual aid and assistance to family members.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes prohibitions target organized smuggling, penalties increased to target organized crime, and s. 117 filters out innocent aid.

propositions.text: Legislative statements may supply evidence of a provision's purpose.
propositions.quote: Statements made in the legislature leading up to the enactment of a provision may supply evidence of its purpose

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative statements can evidence a provision's purpose.

propositions.text: Parliamentary debates show 1988 offence motivated by organized large-scale smuggling by sea and concerns about health, safety, and border control.
propositions.quote: The parliamentary debates establish that the original enactment of the offence in 1988 was motivated by incidents of organized large-scale smuggling of undocumented migrants by sea. Concerns were expressed in the debates about protecting the health, safety and security of Canadians and Canadian society, the integrity and efficacy of Canada’s lawful immigration and refugee regimes, and Canada’s ability to control its borders and the domestic and international interests tied to them.

propositions.text: Concerns also included safety of genuine refugees and avoiding prosecution of humanitarian groups.
propositions.quote: Concerns were also expressed about the safety and protection of genuine refugees, and not subjecting humanitarian groups to prosecution.

propositions.text: Minister Bouchard summarized Parliament's purpose to stop large-scale trafficking and avoid loopholes undermining prosecution.
propositions.quote: Then-Minister Benoît Bouchard summarized Parliament’s purpose as follows in the Committee meetings of August 25, 1987: We are going to put a stop to the large-scale trafficking of illegal migrants by smugglers... We cannot let such individuals escape sanction by adding phrases which create insurmountable problems of proof and create gaps through which the unscrupulous would march.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts parliamentary debates showing the 1988 offence aimed to stop large-scale smuggling and protect refugees without prosecuting humanitarian groups.

propositions.text: Parliament did not intend to prosecute humanitarian or family assistance but used Attorney General's consent as a screening mechanism.
propositions.quote: It thus emerges from the 1987 debates that the reason s. 117(1) of the IRPA permits prosecution of those providing humanitarian assistance to fleeing refugees or assistance to close family members is not because Parliament wanted to capture such persons, but because of a drafting dilemma... Parliament agreed that those offering humanitarian assistance and mutual aid were not meant to be prosecuted under s. 117 of the IRPA . However, instead of legislatively exempting such people from potential criminal liability, it sought to screen them out at the prosecution stage by requiring the Attorney General’s consent to prosecute.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament did not intend to prosecute humanitarian or family aid but relied on Attorney General consent to screen prosecutions.

propositions.text: 2001 IRPA debates echoed concerns about criminalizing family and humanitarian aid, with s. 117(4) expected to prevent unintended prosecutions.
propositions.quote: The debates on the enactment of the IRPA in 2001 echo these preoccupations... The government’s response was that these fears were misplaced because they focused exclusively on s. 117(1) and overlooked s. 117(4) which was expected to prevent these and other unintended prosecutions.

propositions.text: Parliamentary debate excerpts show concern about prosecuting humanitarian workers or family helpers, with assurances about Attorney General's consent safeguard.
propositions.quote: Mr. John McCallum: ... if you read that literally, it looks like some of these people who are helping refugees could be prosecuted... Ms. Joan Atkinson: ... Subclause 117(4) is what’s in the current act... It is in place ... and as Daniel has said, there has been no prosecution of anyone who was involved in trying to help refugees come to Canada. That is the safeguard.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts 2001 debates showing concerns about prosecuting humanitarian or family aid, with s. 117(4) as a safeguard.

propositions.text: Parliament knew s. 117 caught humanitarian and family aid but relied on Attorney General's discretion as a safeguard against inappropriate prosecutions.
propositions.quote: These excerpts from the parliamentary debates make it clear that Parliament understood that s. 117(1) criminalized assistance to family members and humanitarian assistance, and was relying on ministerial discretion to prevent prosecution... defended this overreach ... on the basis that the Attorney General’s permission under s. 117(4) would be an adequate “safeguard” against inappropriate prosecutions.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Parliament relied on Attorney General discretion to prevent prosecution of humanitarian and family aid despite s. 117's broad wording.

propositions.text: Government conceded s. 117(1) was broad enough to catch family and humanitarian aid but intended to exclude them via Attorney General's authorization requirement.
propositions.quote: In sum, we may fairly infer the following from the debate surrounding the adoption of s. 117 of the IRPA : From the beginning, the government conceded that the words of s. 117(1) had been cast broadly enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance to undocumented migrants... The risk would be alleviated... by the requirement that the Attorney General authorize prosecutions under s. 117(4) of the IRPA .

paragraphs.summary: The court infers government conceded s. 117(1) was broad but relied on Attorney General authorization to exclude family and humanitarian aid.

propositions.text: Purpose of s. 117 is to criminalize organized crime-related smuggling, not simple family or humanitarian aid.
propositions.quote: The foregoing considerations establish that the purpose of s. 117 is to criminalize the smuggling of people into Canada in the context of organized crime, and does not extend to permitting prosecution for simply assisting family or providing humanitarian or mutual aid to undocumented entrants to Canada.

propositions.text: A broad punitive goal prosecuting persons unconnected to organized crime is inconsistent with Parliament’s purpose.
propositions.quote: A broad punitive goal that would prosecute persons with no connection to and no furtherance of organized crime is not consistent with Parliament’s purpose as evinced by the text of s. 117 read together with Canada’s international commitments, s. 117 ’s role within the IRPA , the IRPA ’s objects, the history of s. 117 , and the parliamentary debates.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 aims to criminalize organized crime smuggling, not simple family or humanitarian aid, consistent with Parliament's purpose.

propositions.text: Whether s. 117 goes too far and interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective.
propositions.quote: I now turn to the scope of s. 117 of the IRPA to see whether it “goes too far and interferes with some conduct that bears no connection to its objective”: Bedford, at para. 101.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue whether s. 117 overreaches and interferes with unrelated conduct.

propositions.text: Scope of s. 117(1) is plain and unambiguous, criminalizing organizing, inducing, aiding or abetting undocumented entry.
propositions.quote: The scope of s. 117(1) is plain. The provision admits of no ambiguity... s. 117(1), which unambiguously make it an offence to “organize, induce, aid or abet” the undocumented entry.

propositions.text: Parliament knew s. 117(1) was overbroad, catching humanitarian, mutual and family assistance, but relied on Attorney General not prosecuting them.
propositions.quote: Parliament itself understood when it enacted s. 117 that the provision’s reach exceeded its purpose by catching those who provide humanitarian, mutual and family assistance to asylum-seekers coming to Canada, but argued that this overbreadth was not a problem because the Attorney General would not permit the prosecution of such people.

propositions.text: Interpreting s. 117(1) to exclude humanitarian, mutual or family assistance would violate the rule of statutory interpretation requiring ordinary grammatical meaning.
propositions.quote: To adopt this suggestion would violate the rule of statutory interpretation that the meaning of the words of the provision should be read in their “grammatical and ordinary sense”: Sullivan, at p. 28.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) unambiguous and overbroad, catching humanitarian and family aid, and cannot be narrowly interpreted to exclude them.

propositions.text: s. 117(1) appears to criminalize conduct unrelated to its objective, raising overbreadth concerns.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117(1) appears to criminalize some conduct that bears no relation to its objective, raising the spectre that s. 117 as a whole is overbroad.

propositions.text: Whether Attorney General's consent under s. 117(4) saves s. 117 from overbreadth by narrowing its scope.
propositions.quote: The remaining question is whether the requirement under s. 117(4) that the Attorney General authorize prosecution saves s. 117 from the charge or overbreadth by effectively narrowing the scope of s. 117(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117(1) is overbroad and questions if Attorney General consent under s. 117(4) cures this.

propositions.text: s. 117(4) does not cure overbreadth; ministerial discretion does not negate criminalization beyond Parliament's object.
propositions.quote: In my view, s. 117(4) does not cure the overbreadth problem created by s. 117(1). Ministerial discretion, whether conscientiously exercised or not, does not negate the fact that s. 117(1) criminalizes conduct beyond Parliament’s object...

propositions.text: Possibility of Attorney General consenting to prosecute humanitarian or family aid engages s. 7 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: So long as the provision is on the books, and so long as it is not impossible that the Attorney General could consent to prosecute... This possibility alone engages s. 7 of the Charter.

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion does not excuse breach of constitutional duty (R. v. Anderson).
propositions.quote: as this Court unanimously noted in R. v. Anderson... “prosecutorial discretion provides no answer to the breach of a constitutional duty”.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds s. 117(4) does not cure overbreadth; prosecutorial discretion cannot excuse constitutional breaches under s. 7.

propositions.text: Court rejects view that overbreadth problem is only administrative law issue about Attorney General's discretion not to prosecute.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree. As noted, although the purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA was not to capture such persons, nothing in the provision actually enacted disallows it.

propositions.text: Judicial review of Attorney General's discretion under s. 117(4) is not currently available and may be undesirable.
propositions.quote: Further, judicial review of such discretion is not currently available, and there are good reasons why it may not be desirable.

propositions.text: Judicial review of prosecutorial discretion risks disrupting adversarial system roles (R. v. Anderson).
propositions.quote: As the Court observed in Anderson, judicial oversight of Crown decisions whether to prosecute puts at risk the discrete roles of different actors in our adversarial system...

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects that overbreadth is only an administrative law issue and notes judicial review of prosecutorial discretion is limited and risky.

propositions.text: Judicial review of Attorney General's decision under s. 117(4) may have undesirable consequences for other federal statutes with similar clauses.
propositions.quote: It may also be noted that judicial review of the Attorney General’s decision to authorize prosecution under s. 117(4) may have undesirable consequences for other federal statutes in which a similar clause is present...

propositions.text: Judicial review does not resolve constitutional non-conformity of s. 117(1).
propositions.quote: At this point, it suffices to note that judicial review does not answer the constitutional non-conformity of s. 117(1) .

paragraphs.summary: The court notes judicial review of Attorney General decisions may affect other statutes and does not fix s. 117(1)'s constitutional issues.

propositions.text: s. 117 of the IRPA is overbroad; next issue is whether overbreadth is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117 of the IRPA is overbroad. The remaining issue is whether this overbreadth is justified under s. 1 of the Charter as a reasonable measure in a free and democratic society.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is overbroad and must consider if this is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: Appellants assert s. 117 violates s. 7 by gross disproportionality, vagueness, and equality principles of fundamental justice.
propositions.quote: In addition to the overbreadth claim, some of the appellants assert that s. 117 offends s. 7 by depriving persons of liberty in a manner that violates the principles of fundamental justice against gross disproportionality and vagueness. They also claim that equal treatment under the law is a principle of fundamental justice within the meaning of s. 7 , and that s. 117 violates it.

propositions.text: Court finds it unnecessary to consider these arguments given conclusion on overbreadth.
propositions.quote: In view of my conclusion that s. 117 is overbroad, I find it unnecessary to consider these arguments.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue s. 117 violates s. 7 by disproportionality, vagueness, and equality; court declines to consider these further.

propositions.text: s. 1 justification test from R. v. Oakes requires pressing and substantial objective.
propositions.quote: The test to determine whether infringement of a right may be constitutionally justified under s. 1 of the Charter was set out in R. v. Oakes... The first step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the Crown has demonstrated a pressing and substantial objective

propositions.text: Broad purpose of s. 117 is to combat organized crime-related people smuggling without criminalizing family, mutual, or humanitarian aid.
propositions.quote: The broad purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA is to combat organized crime-related people smuggling, without criminalizing family assistance, mutual aid or humanitarian aid to asylum-seekers coming to Canada.

propositions.text: This objective is pressing and substantial.
propositions.quote: This objective is clearly pressing and substantial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the s. 1 test requires a pressing objective, which s. 117's purpose to combat organized crime smuggling meets.

propositions.text: Second step of s. 1 analysis requires rational connection between objective and law's limit on rights.
propositions.quote: The second step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the legislative objective is rationally connected to the limit the law imposes on the right at issue.

propositions.text: Not all applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to its objective; some catch humanitarian, mutual, and family aid.
propositions.quote: Not all applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to the legislative object; notably, s. 117 of the IRPA , as discussed, catches mutual and family as well as humanitarian aid which I earlier concluded was not Parliament’s object to criminalize.

propositions.text: Since some applications are rationally connected, rational connection stage is satisfied.
propositions.quote: However, since other applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to the legislative object, this suffices to satisfy the rational connection stage of the analysis: Heywood, at p. 803.

propositions.text: Rational connection requires rational link, not complete correspondence (Heywood).
propositions.quote: A rational connection, not a complete rational correspondence, is all this branch of Oakes requires.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 partially rationally connected to its objective, satisfying s. 1's rational connection step.

propositions.text: The third step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the offending law is tailored to its objective
propositions.quote: The third step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the offending law is tailored to its objective: R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713.

propositions.text: A law that goes too far challenges minimal impairment
propositions.quote: Evidently, where a law goes too far, it is a challenge to satisfy minimal impairment.

propositions.text: In Heywood, Cory J. concluded the law was overly broad and failed minimal impairment
propositions.quote: In Heywood, Cory J. concluded (at p. 803) that “for the same reasons that [the law] is overly broad, it fails the minimal impairment branch of the s. 1 analysis”.

propositions.text: The record here shows that overbreadth does not always mean failure of minimal impairment
propositions.quote: The record here shows why that will not always necessarily be the case.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 1 minimal impairment step, cites Heywood's finding of overbreadth failing minimal impairment, but notes overbreadth does not always fail minimal impairment.

propositions.text: The provision is overbroad but minimally impairing because no better alternative existed
propositions.quote: The Crown’s position appears to be that even though the provision is overbroad, it is nevertheless minimally impairing, because although imperfect, there was no better alternative.
